translationRepairs: Liu Bei continued, I reckoned Sun Quan's worry lay north and that he would need me as an ally, so I went without hesitation.
I believed Sun Quan’s defenses were directed northward and that he would need me as an ally, so I decided to go without hesitation.

The Chinese remains in Liu Bei’s first-person speech. The existing narrative tag breaks the quotation grammatically; this revision restores the speaker and renders 所防在北 as defenses directed northward.
〈Jiang Ji’s Treatise on Myriad Affairs notes that Xu Shao’s praises and censures were skewed—he boosted Fan Zizhao and played down Xu Shao the younger.
〈Jiang Ji’s Treatise on Myriad Affairs notes that Xu Shao’s praises and censures were skewed—he boosted Fan Zizhao and played down Xu Wenxiu.

許文休 identifies the second man by the courtesy name Wenxiu; it does not describe a younger man also named Xu Shao. The proposed wording follows the exact name form in the source without inventing a personal name.

He usually wore a plain scholar’s headcloth to meet the Administrator of Fufeng, who said: “Though Duke Ai was unworthy, he still served Confucius as minister; Liuxia Hui would not leave his parents’ state—I wish to press you to take office as Clerk of Merit—what say you?”

He usually wore a plain scholar’s headcloth to meet the Administrator of Fufeng, who said: “Though Duke Ai was unworthy, he still had Confucius as his minister; Liuxia Hui would not leave his parents’ state—I wish to press you to take office as Clerk of Merit—what say you?”
臣仲尼 makes Confucius Duke Ai’s minister; the existing literal translation reverses that relationship.
〈The Records of Huayang Country states that Du came from Guanghan and held the post of provincial attendant.〉
〈The Chronicles of Huayang records that Du was from Guanghan and served as a provincial attendant.〉
華陽國志 is the work conventionally titled Chronicles of Huayang. The existing 'Records of Huayang Country' mistakes 國志 for an ordinary phrase rather than part of the title.
Liang replied: “When the sovereign was at Gong’an he feared Cao Cao’s strength to the north, Sun Quan’s pressure to the east, and Sun Lady brewing trouble at his elbow;
Liang replied: “When the sovereign was at Gong’an he feared Cao Cao’s strength to the north, Sun Quan’s pressure to the east, and Lady Sun brewing trouble at his elbow;
孫夫人 is the title Lady Sun; 'Sun Lady' reverses normal English title order.
Cao Cao’s barb is wounded vanity, not acute analysis.
Even if someone else had advised him, as Emperor Wu of Wei believed, would that make him any less capable?

The sentence continues the defense of rulers who act on good advice. It asks rhetorically whether receiving counsel diminishes Liu Bei; the existing wording instead invents a comment about Cao Cao’s vanity.
Pei dismisses Cao’s remark as spite, not truth.〉
Those were merely bitter words born of wounded pride, not a fair assessment of the facts.〉

The Chinese characterizes the preceding remark as residual language of shame and resentment and contrasts it with a measured judgment of reality. This revision preserves that logic without inserting named agents.
His son Miao inherited a Marquis Within the Passes and rose to Colonel of the Chariots and prefect of Hanyang.
His son Miao was granted the rank of Marquis Within the Passes and rose to become Colonel of the Chariots and Administrator of Hanyang.
賜 means that Miao received a new grant, not that he inherited Fa Zheng’s posthumous title. The revision also renders 太守 consistently as Administrator.
Zhuge Liang and Fa Zheng differed in temperament yet respected each other’s office.
Though Zhuge Liang and Fa Zheng differed in their tastes and values, they respected each other’s commitment to the public good.
公義 denotes public righteousness or the public good, not an office. The revision gives 相取 its reciprocal sense in natural English.
Once Liu Bei took the throne he aimed east at Sun Quan to wipe away Guan Yu’s defeat—counselors pleaded in vain.
Once Liu Bei took the throne, he prepared to march east against Sun Quan and avenge the humiliation of Guan Yu’s defeat; his ministers repeatedly remonstrated, but he ignored them all.
復關羽之恥 means to avenge the shame associated with Guan Yu’s defeat. The revision retains that concrete context while restoring the explicit force of 群臣多諫，一不從.
